learn.intro: From War Communism and the NEP to Stalin's Five-Year Plans and collectivisation, then Khrushchev's Virgin Lands, Brezhnev's stagnation and Gorbachev's failed reforms: how did the command economy develop, and why did it fall behind?

blocks.p: The Decree on Land (October 1917) let peasants take landlords' estates. Large-scale industry was nationalised in June 1918, and a Supreme Council of the National Economy (VSNKh) was set up to run it.

War Communism (1918–21) put the economy on a war footing: grain was requisitioned from peasants, private trade was banned, and money almost lost its value. Industrial output collapsed to a fraction of its 1913 level, and the famine of 1921–22 killed about 5 million people. Peasant risings and the Kronstadt revolt showed the policy had to change.

The New Economic Policy (NEP, March 1921) replaced requisitioning with a tax in kind, allowed peasants to sell surplus grain and allowed small private businesses ('Nepmen'). The state kept the 'commanding heights' — heavy industry, banks, foreign trade. By about 1926 output had recovered to roughly pre-war levels, but the 'scissors crisis' (1923) and the grain procurement crisis of 1927–28 showed the tension between peasants and the state.

State control of industry and agriculture grew: Gosplan (state planning, 1921) and the party argued over whether to keep the NEP (Bukharin) or industrialise rapidly at the peasants' expense (the Left, later Stalin).

sections.title: 2. Industry and agriculture in the Stalin era

blocks.p: The Five-Year Plans: the First Plan (1928–32, declared complete in four years) set huge targets for heavy industry. New industrial cities such as Magnitogorsk and the Dnieper dam were built. Coal output rose from about 35 million tonnes (1928) to about 128 million (1937), and steel from about 4 million to about 18 million tonnes. The Second Plan (1933–37) added transport such as the Moscow Metro; Stakhanov's record coal shift (August 1935) launched the Stakhanovite movement.

Preparing for war: the Third Plan (1938–41) switched resources to armaments — defence took about a third of the budget by 1940. After the German invasion in 1941, over 1,500 large factories were moved east to the Urals and Siberia.

Agricultural collectivisation and its impact: from late 1929 peasants were forced into collective farms (kolkhozy). Stalin declared the 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class'; about 1.8 million people were deported as kulaks in 1930–31, and many more were shot or died. Peasants slaughtered their animals rather than hand them over, so livestock numbers roughly halved. Grain procurement continued during the famine of 1932–33, which killed an estimated 5–7 million people, especially in Ukraine and Kazakhstan. By the late 1930s almost all farms were collectivised and controlled through Machine Tractor Stations.
Recovery from war after 1945: the Fourth Plan (1946–50) rebuilt heavy industry quickly using forced labour and reparations, but agriculture stayed weak and there was famine in 1946–47.

sections.title: 3. Changing priorities for industry and agriculture, 1953–91

blocks.p: Khrushchev promised more consumer goods, light industry and chemicals (for fertilisers, plastics and fabrics), while keeping heavy industry and the space and arms programmes. Housing construction expanded rapidly.

Investment in agriculture and the Virgin Lands Scheme (from 1954): young volunteers ploughed tens of millions of hectares of steppe in Kazakhstan and Siberia. The 1956 harvest was a record, but soil erosion and poor planning followed, and after the bad harvest of 1963 the USSR had to import grain. Price rises led to riots at Novocherkassk in 1962.

The attempts at reform 1964–91: Kosygin's reform (1965) gave factories more freedom and used profit as a measure, but it was diluted by planners. Under Brezhnev agriculture received about a quarter of all investment, yet the USSR imported grain from the 1970s. Growth slowed sharply, military spending took a very large share of output, and the 'second economy' (black market) grew. High oil prices in the 1970s hid the problems.

The impact of Gorbachev's economic reforms 1985–91: 'acceleration' (uskorenie) and the anti-alcohol campaign (1985) cut state revenue; the Law on State Enterprise (1987) and the Law on Cooperatives (1988) loosened planning without creating a working market. With falling oil prices after 1986, shortages, rationing, budget deficits and inflation grew, and output fell in 1990–91. Plans for a rapid move to a market (the '500 Days' programme, 1990) were not adopted.

vocab.def: An economy run by central state plans, not the market.
1918–21 policy of requisitioning, nationalisation and banning private trade.
1921 New Economic Policy allowing limited private trade.
Forcing peasants into state-controlled collective farms.
A 'rich' peasant — in practice any peasant labelled an enemy.
Khrushchev's scheme to farm new land in Kazakhstan and Siberia.
Illegal private trade and the black market.

misconceptions.wrong: The NEP was a return to capitalism.
misconceptions.right: The state kept the 'commanding heights'; Lenin called it a temporary retreat.

misconceptions.wrong: The Five-Year Plans met all their targets.
misconceptions.right: Heavy industry grew fast, but many targets were missed and statistics were often exaggerated.

misconceptions.wrong: Kulaks were a clearly defined wealthy class.
misconceptions.right: The label was applied loosely to anyone who resisted collectivisation.

misconceptions.wrong: The Soviet economy collapsed only because of Gorbachev.
misconceptions.right: Growth had slowed since the 1970s; his reforms made the shortages worse.

matching.title: Match the period to the economic policy

evidence.q: Give precise evidence about the impact of collectivisation.
evidence.model: About 1.8 million people were deported as kulaks in 1930–31; livestock numbers roughly halved as peasants slaughtered animals; the famine of 1932–33 killed an estimated 5–7 million, especially in Ukraine and Kazakhstan; by the late 1930s nearly all farms were kolkhozy controlled through Machine Tractor Stations.

flashcards.q: Why did Lenin replace War Communism with the NEP?
flashcards.a: Output collapse, famine of 1921–22, peasant risings and Kronstadt showed the regime could not survive without peasant cooperation.

flashcards.q: What did the Five-Year Plans achieve?
flashcards.a: Huge growth in heavy industry (coal about 35m to 128m tonnes 1928–37, steel about 4m to 18m), new cities, war production — at great human cost.
Secure grain for the cities and exports, fund industry, end the 'kulak' threat and bring the peasants under party control.

flashcards.q: How successful was the Virgin Lands Scheme?
flashcards.a: Record harvest in 1956, but soil erosion and poor planning followed; grain had to be imported after 1963.

flashcards.q: Why did the economy stagnate under Brezhnev?
flashcards.a: Reforms diluted, huge military spending, waste in agriculture, black market; oil money hid the problems.

flashcards.q: Why did Gorbachev's economic reforms fail?
flashcards.a: They weakened central planning without creating a market; anti-alcohol campaign and falling oil prices cut revenue; shortages and inflation followed.
